title: How To Make A Noise: A Comprehensive Guide to Synthesizer Programming
author: Simon Cann
path: E:\pdf\music\Cann Simon How to make a noise _ a comprehensive guide to synthesizer programming Coombe Hill.pdf
card_summary: Simon Cann's hands-on synth-programming manual teaches subtractive, FM, wave-sequencing, and additive synthesis by building real patches (bass, pads, leads, drums) on six software synths, walking through oscillators, envelopes, filters, modulation, and FX one concept at a time.
page_summary: How To Make A Noise is a practitioner's synthesis primer built entirely around making usable sounds rather than abstract signal theory. Cann (a working sound designer) structures the book as a sequence of twelve chapters plus four 'refill' supplements: Getting Started, Envelopes, Filters, Sound Sources, Modulation (concept, then in-practice), Frequency Modulation Synthesis (with a Surge-specific supplement), Wave-Sequencing, Additive Synthesis, FX, Putting It All Together, and Building Patches, followed by refills on arpeggiators/step sequencers, 'pushing the sonic envelope,' and synthetic drum/percussion design. Each concept — ADSR vs. DAHDSR vs. DASSDSR envelope shapes, low-pass/high-pass/band-pass/notch/formant/comb filter types, basic wave shapes (sine, sawtooth, square/pulse, triangle, noise) and their combination via doubling, layering, and hard sync — is explained and then immediately demonstrated as an audible patch on one of six late-2000s/2010s software synths: Camel Audio Cameleon 5000, Big Tick Rhino, Vember Audio Surge, reFX Vanguard, Wusik Wusikstation, and Cakewalk Z3TA+. The FM chapter is unusually thorough for a 'basics' book: it covers operator/carrier-modulator relationships, 1:1 vs. varying ratios, parallel vs. cascading operators, and building a first FM patch from scratch, essentially teaching the same conceptual territory as Yamaha DX7-style synthesis without requiring DX7 hardware. The additive chapter honestly flags 'Warning!! Mathematics Ahead' before walking through building square, sawtooth, and triangle waves from summed sine partials — a direct, worked illustration of Fourier synthesis. The book is written for musicians and producers who own a software synth and want to move past factory presets to sound design they understand, not for DSP engineers; there is no code, no math beyond arithmetic ratios, and no discussion of how any of this is implemented in a signal-processing sense. It is squarely a 'what knob does what, and why does it sound like that' book, organized so a reader can skip to the synthesis method they need (subtractive vs. FM vs. additive vs. wave-sequencing) independently. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is high-value conceptual scaffolding rather than implementation help: it will not show how to write a JSFX oscillator or filter, but it gives a working vocabulary and mental model — what an ADSR stage should sound like, what a resonant low-pass sweep should sound like, how FM operator ratios generate inharmonic vs. harmonic spectra — that is exactly what's needed to know whether a hand-written JSFX synth 'sounds right' before worrying about whether it is DSP-correct. It is a good source of target patches (basses, leads, pads, plucks, synthetic kick/snare/hats) to try to reproduce once a JSFX synth has its first audible note, per the project's own 'one audible note before building anything else' rule.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: High — the clearest general synthesis-concepts primer in the library (oscillators/envelopes/filters/FM/additive/modulation), though it teaches ears-and-patches, not DSP code or JSFX specifics.

title: Johann Sebastian Bach's Art of Fugue: Performance Practice Based on German Eighteenth-Century Theory
author: Ewald Demeyere

card_summary: Demeyere reconstructs how Bach's late, abstract keyboard-independent counterpoint cycle Die Kunst der Fuge should actually sound, grounding tempo, articulation, ornamentation and instrumentation choices in period German theoretical treatises rather than modern performance convention.
page_summary: This is a musicological monograph (Leuven University Press, 2017) arguing that the performance of Bach's Art of Fugue (BWV 1080) — a set of fourteen fugues and four canons on a single subject, left without specified instrumentation and unfinished at Bach's death — has been distorted by two centuries of Romantic and modernist assumptions about what 'abstract' or 'purely intellectual' contrapuntal music should sound like. Demeyere's method is to reconstruct period German performance practice from eighteenth-century treatises (Quantz, C.P.E. Bach, Türk, Kirnberger, and others in Bach's own circle) and apply those norms — tempo relationships between movements, articulation of subject entries, appropriate ornamentation, notes inégales-adjacent rhythmic inflection, and the vexed question of whether the work was conceived for a single keyboard, two keyboards, or an unspecified consort — directly to the Art of Fugue's individual movements. Chapters proceed roughly through the theoretical framework (rhetoric, affect, and fugal theory in the German tradition) and then through practice-oriented analysis of specific contrapuncti, including the famously unfinished final quadruple fugue (Contrapunctus XIV) and the disputed status of the 'mirror fugues.' The book is written for advanced keyboardists, harpsichordists/organists, conductors, and musicologists already fluent in species counterpoint and historical performance practice (HIP) debates — it assumes score-reading fluency and familiarity with fugal terminology (subject, answer, countersubject, stretto, augmentation, inversion) throughout, and is not an introduction to Bach or to fugue as a form. For SYNTHBUILDER specifically, this book is essentially irrelevant to synthesis, DSP, or plugin building — it is a historical-performance-practice study of a specific keyboard repertoire, not music theory in the compositional-craft sense and not remotely about sound technology. Its value to Ted's broader practice is as deep Bach/counterpoint background (useful if a future SYNTHBUILDER or FUGUEJUKEBOX-style project wants to generate or arrange fugal material with historically informed phrasing) rather than as a synthesis or chiptune-programming resource. It belongs on the showcase page as music-history/Bach-scholarship depth, not as a technical manual.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a historical-performance-practice study of Bach's counterpoint, not synthesis or DSP; useful only as deep Bach/fugue background for future composition-generation work.

card_summary: Andreas Loewe's Brill monograph reads Bach's St John Passion movement by movement as Lutheran theology set to music, tracing how the libretto's chorales, arias and turba choruses embody eighteenth-century Leipzig devotional and doctrinal concerns.
page_summary: This is a scholarly theological-musicological commentary on one of Bach's two surviving Passion settings, the St John Passion (BWV 245, first performed Good Friday 1724 in Leipzig). Loewe's central argument is that the Passion cannot be fully understood as 'just' a musical masterpiece: its text (assembled from the Gospel of John, chorale verses, and newly written poetic meditations, likely with Bach's own theological input) is a carefully constructed piece of Lutheran devotional theology, and the music's rhetorical and affective choices — where a chorale interrupts the narrative, how the turba (crowd) choruses are harmonized, which arias comment on which narrative moments — are themselves theological arguments. The book proceeds through the work's structure, contextualizing Bach's Leipzig cantorate, the liturgical role of the Good Friday Vespers service the Passion was written for, the textual sources and revisions Bach made across several performing versions, and then close readings of individual movements that connect musical gesture (key choice, instrumentation, motivic word-painting) to specific points of Lutheran Christology and soteriology. It is written for musicologists, theologians, and advanced choral conductors/performers who already know the piece and want its doctrinal substructure explained, not as a general-audience introduction to the Passion or to Bach. For SYNTHBUILDER this book has no direct technical relevance — it is theology and text-music analysis, not synthesis, DSP, or sound design, and its subject (a large-scale choral/orchestral sacred work) is about as far from NES-chip-accurate chiptune programming as the library gets. Its place on the showcase page is purely as evidence of the depth of Ted's Bach collection alongside the more practically synth-relevant titles, useful background if a future project ever wanted to arrange or chiptune-ify Bach vocal material with attention to its original structure and meaning.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — theological/textual analysis of a choral-orchestral sacred work; no synthesis or DSP content, general Bach-scholarship background only.

Each contributor is assigned three tasks within a specific subject area: (1) summarize the significant and controversial research of the past thirty to fifty years — examples cited include the debate over Friedrich Smend's Neue Bach-Ausgabe edition of the B minor Mass, Friedrich Blume's conclusions about Bach's religious commitment following the 'new chronology' of the cantatas (established via paper and handwriting studies), Joshua Rifkin's controversial one-voice-per-part reconstruction of Bach's vocal forces, and the rediscovery of the Berlin Sing-Akademie manuscript collection in Kiev after the Cold War; (2) critically analyze current research opening new methodological ground, such as Martin Jarvis's contested forensic-handwriting claim that Anna Magdalena Bach composed the cello suites, and ongoing work tracing Bach's use of the Lutheran chorale tradition; and (3) identify areas still needing investigation. The result is a state-of-the-field survey organized by topic (chronology and sources, theology and text, instrumental and vocal genres, reception and performance practice) rather than a biography or a listener's guide, deliberately written to orient a researcher entering Bach studies toward the live scholarly controversies rather than settled facts. For SYNTHBUILDER this is not a technical resource at all — no synthesis, DSP, or sound-programming content — but as general music-scholarship background it is the single best-organized map in the library of what current Bach research actually argues about (chronology, authorship, performance practice), which is useful context if Ted's other Bach-adjacent projects (e.g. CHIPPEDONBACH, referenced in SYNTHBUILDER's own docs) ever need to justify a source-critical choice about which version of a Bach piece to arrange or chiptune.

The study's theoretical scaffolding combines the Task-Technology Fit (TTF) model with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which together model the causal chain from perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use through to actual usage behavior — a standard information-systems research framework, applied here to music production tools rather than business software. The empirical base is a survey of 838 completed responses from heavy metal and hard rock artists specifically (chosen, per the abstract, because that genre community has been an early and heavy adopter of home-studio DAW workflows as an alternative to commercial studios), analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The article's framing draws on prior work (cited: Persson) arguing that affordable DAWs and home recording equipment created real competition for commercial studios and forced a re-evaluation of what gets recorded at home versus in a professional facility, and by whom. The piece is written for an audience of information-systems and media-technology researchers, not musicians or producers — it does not teach DAW use, mixing, or recording technique, and contains no discussion of specific DAW software features. For SYNTHBUILDER this article is essentially irrelevant: it is organizational/adoption-behavior research about why musicians choose DAWs, not a technical, DSP, or plugin-development resource, and it says nothing about REAPER, JSFX, VST3, or synthesis. page_summary: The Recording Engineer's Handbook (2nd edition, Course Technology/Cengage, 2009) is a comprehensively practical, chapter-by-chapter reference for the craft of audio recording, organized to mirror an actual session workflow. Chapter 1, 'How Microphones Work,' covers dynamic, ribbon, and condenser microphone designs, condenser myths and operational hints, phantom power, and the full vocabulary of mic specifications (sensitivity, overload characteristics, frequency response, self-noise, polar patterns, proximity effect) plus specialty mics (shotgun, lavalier, PZM, wireless, stereo, parabolic) and accessories (pop filters, windscreens, shock mounts). Chapter 2 surveys named classic and modern microphone models (Neumann U47/U67/M49/KM84/U87, AKG C12/C451/414, Shure SM57, Sennheiser MD421/441, Electro-Voice RE20, and current affordable equivalents) with interview material from mic designer David Bock. Chapter 3 covers basic recording equipment — mic preamps (vintage vs. modern, setup, direct injection) and compressor/limiters. Chapter 4, 'DAW Recording,' is the book's most directly relevant chapter to SYNTHBUILDER's domain: getting sound into a computer, how ADCs and DACs work, latency, FireWire-vs-USB tradeoffs, and headroom/gain-staging, including an interview with a Digidesign product manager. Later chapters cover stereo miking techniques (coincident, spaced, Decca Tree, near-coincident, baffled-omni pairs), multichannel tracking and phase-checking (by ear, oscilloscope plug-in, or phase meter), drum-kit preparation and miking (with an interview with 'Drum Doctor' Ross Garfield), and individual-instrument miking technique across a wide instrument list. The book is written for working and aspiring recording/mix engineers — assumes no DSP or programming background, is entirely equipment- and technique-focused rather than theoretical, and teaches craft judgment (mic choice, placement, gain staging) rather than synthesis or plugin construction. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is moderately useful adjacent knowledge: the DAW-recording chapter's coverage of latency, ADC/DAC behavior, and headroom/gain-staging is directly relevant to getting clean signal in and out of REAPER when testing a JSFX synth, and the general audio-engineering vocabulary (signal chain, gain staging, monitoring) is useful context — but the book does not address synthesis, DSP coding, or plugin formats (JSFX/VST3) at all, so its use is as supporting audio-engineering literacy rather than a synth-building resource.

Its explicit coverage of three distinct areas — general synthesizer fundamentals (oscillators, envelopes, filters, modulation, in the analog/subtractive vocabulary standard to the era), the DX7 specifically (FM operator-based synthesis, at the time a genuinely new and confusing paradigm for most musicians), sampling devices (early hardware samplers), and the then-brand-new MIDI protocol — makes it a useful time-capsule of exactly what a working musician needed to learn in 1985-86 to use the generation of gear that dominated pop, film, and video-game (including early NES-adjacent) music production. It is written for musicians and hobbyists with no electronics or programming background, in the plain, non-technical 'basics' tradition typical of Amsco's instructional series. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book's chief value is historical/conceptual: it explains FM synthesis and MIDI from the exact era and mindset that also produced the NES's own sound hardware and the early-digital-synth sound SYNTHBUILDER is chasing, and its DX7/FM section is a good plain-language companion to the more code-focused FM material in Simon Cann's book. It teaches no DSP math or programming, but as an accessible period-accurate primer on 'what FM synthesis actually is and why MIDI exists,' it is a reasonable on-ramp before tackling JSFX implementation.

page_summary: Published by Rock Tech Publications in 1984, The Rock Synthesizer Manual is a period document of early-1980s analog/voltage-controlled synthesizer practice, written specifically for rock and pop musicians (rather than academic electronic-music composers) who needed to understand the generation of standalone hardware synths — Moog, ARP, Oberheim, Roland, Sequential Circuits-era instruments — that had become central to the era's music. Its table of contents runs through 'Electronic Sound' fundamentals in a logical build-up: basics of sound (waveform, frequency, amplitude), electronic sound sources (oscillators), voltage control (the defining paradigm of the era's analog synths, where every parameter is controlled by a variable voltage rather than digital data), voltage-controlled amplifiers (VCAs), envelope generation, filtering, modulation, keyboard controllers, sequencers, sample-and-hold circuits (a classic source of the era's 'random arpeggio' textures), footpedal controllers and footswitches, and programmable patch memory (a genuinely new feature at the time, replacing patch cables/knob-recall with digitally stored parameter presets). The book teaches the voltage-control paradigm directly rather than through any particular manufacturer's synth, in the tradition of period primers aimed at giving working musicians (not engineers) a functional map of what each module does and how to combine them into usable sounds. It predates MIDI's full dominance and is squarely a hardware-modular/voltage-control-era text rather than a software or DAW-plugin one. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book is directly useful as core subtractive-synthesis conceptual grounding — VCO/VCF/VCA/envelope/LFO signal flow is exactly the architecture a JSFX subtractive synth needs to implement, and the book explains each stage's musical function clearly and concisely without assuming DSP programming knowledge. It won't show code, but as a plain-language explanation of what a filter cutoff or an envelope's decay stage is supposed to do to a sound, it pairs well with Cann's more patch-oriented book and Pirkle's DSP-implementation book, filling the conceptual middle ground between the two.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Medium-High — a clear, non-technical explanation of the VCO/VCF/VCA/envelope/LFO subtractive-synthesis signal chain that any JSFX subtractive synth needs to implement, though it teaches concepts, not code.

title: Game Sound: An Introduction to the History, Theory, and Practice of Video Game Music and Sound Design
author: Karen Collins
path: E:\pdf\music\Karen Collins Game sound_ an introduction to the history theory and practice of video game music and sound design The MIT Press.pdf
card_summary: Karen Collins's MIT Press textbook is the foundational academic survey of video game audio, tracing the technical history from early arcade/console sound chips (including the NES) through MIDI-era and modern interactive scoring, alongside theoretical frameworks for game-sound analysis.
page_summary: Game Sound (MIT Press, 2008) is widely regarded as the founding academic textbook of the field now called ludomusicology — the scholarly study of video game music and sound. Karen Collins structures the book to serve simultaneously as a history, a theory primer, and a practical introduction: it opens with the technical history of game audio from its earliest electromechanical and arcade origins through the 8-bit and 16-bit console era (where the specific sound-chip architectures — square/pulse/triangle/noise channels of systems like the NES's 2A03 APU, FM synthesis chips in arcade and Sega hardware, and the constraints they imposed on composers — are central subject matter directly relevant to chiptune practice), through the CD-audio/MIDI transition and into contemporary adaptive and interactive scoring techniques (horizontal re-sequencing, vertical layering, dynamic mixing responding to game state). Alongside this technical/historical track, the book develops theoretical vocabulary for analyzing how game sound functions — diegetic vs. non-diegetic sound, the relationship between sound design and player agency/interactivity (a concern absent from film-sound theory, which the book explicitly positions itself against/alongside), and sound's role in gameplay feedback, immersion, and genre signaling. It closes with practice-oriented material on the actual process of composing and implementing game audio, including collaboration between composers and programmers/sound designers. The book is written for an academic audience (game studies, musicology, media studies students and scholars) but is broadly accessible to informed general readers and industry practitioners; it assumes no advanced music theory but does assume seriousness about game audio as a subject worthy of sustained analysis. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is one of the most directly relevant non-technical books in the library: its historical treatment of 8-bit sound-chip architecture and the compositional constraints composers worked under is exactly the domain knowledge needed to make NES-tone-accurate chiptune choices meaningfully (not just imitate the timbre but understand why NES composers wrote the way they did given 2A03 channel limitations), and its interactive/adaptive-audio theory is useful if SYNTHBUILDER's REAPER work ever extends toward game-responsive audio rather than static tracks.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: High — the standard academic history of game/chiptune sound-chip architecture (including NES APU constraints) plus theory of interactive audio; essential context, though not a code/DSP manual.

From there the book proceeds through essays by leading early-music scholars covering genres (plainchant, polyphony, the mass and motet, secular song traditions), regional traditions, notational practice, instruments, and major figures across the period, in the reference-companion format of short (2,000-5,000 word) contributions by different specialists rather than a single-author narrative history. It includes illustrations, music examples set by a professional music engraver, and a substantial bibliographic apparatus, aimed at undergraduate and graduate music students, performers of early music, and generally curious readers with some existing music-history background — it assumes familiarity with basic music-historical periodization and some notational literacy but explains specialist terms as needed. For SYNTHBUILDER this has no direct technical relevance — no synthesis, sound technology, or DSP content, and its subject matter (vocal polyphony, plainchant, Renaissance instrumental consort music) is stylistically and technologically about as distant from chiptune synthesis as the library gets. The book likely covers both the album's compositional/conceptual ambitions and its studio-technology choices (the Fairlight's role in Bush's sound, orchestral and folk-instrument layering, the period's emerging digital-recording capabilities), in keeping with the 33 1/3 format's blend of criticism, biography, and production history. Written for informed music fans and critics, not technical producers, it assumes interest in art-pop history rather than DSP or synthesis background. page_summary: Michiel Kamp's Four Ways of Hearing Video Game Music is an academic monograph within the ludomusicology field established by scholars like Karen Collins (also in this library) and the Ludomusicology research network Kamp co-edits (see the companion volume Ludomusicology, also in Ted's collection). The book engages closely with specific games and their scores as case studies to substantiate each listening mode, situating itself within broader film-music and sound-studies theory as much as within game studies specifically. It is written for an academic audience in musicology, media studies, and game studies — it assumes familiarity with core music-theoretical and film-sound-theory vocabulary and is a work of theory-building, not a history or a how-to-compose guide. For SYNTHBUILDER, this book is more conceptually than technically useful: it offers no synthesis, DSP, or programming content, but its close attention to how listeners actually process game audio during interactive play is relevant if SYNTHBUILDER's chiptune work ever moves beyond static tracks toward interactive or game-responsive audio, giving vocabulary for thinking about what a chiptune voice needs to communicate functionally (not just faithfully reproduce NES timbre) within a play context.

card_summary: Will Pirkle's standard textbook (Focal Press/Routledge) for building real synthesizer plugins in C++, covering oscillators, envelope generators, filters (including a full Moog ladder-filter implementation), LFOs, and complete synth-voice architecture across RackAFX, VST3 and Audio Units.
page_summary: Designing Software Synthesizer Plug-Ins in C++ is a 912-page, deeply technical, code-driven textbook by Will Pirkle — author of several widely used Focal Press/Routledge audio-DSP programming books and creator of the free RackAFX plugin-prototyping framework used as this book's primary teaching environment, alongside full coverage of exporting the same DSP code to VST3 and Audio Units plugin formats. The book's approach is to build a complete, working polyphonic software synthesizer incrementally in C++, teaching digital synthesis theory and object-oriented plugin architecture simultaneously: rather than treating synthesis theory and software engineering as separate concerns, each chapter pairs a DSP concept with its concrete C++ class implementation. Visible in the extracted cover and page images are direct code excerpts — delay-line difference equations (dLeftDelayIn/dRightDelayIn feedback calculations), and, strikingly, a full C++ class declaration for CMoogLadderFilter : public CFilter, implementing the specific nonlinear four-pole Moog transistor-ladder filter topology by name — indicating the book teaches not generic textbook filters but specific, musically important circuit models translated into code. Based on its scope and Pirkle's other books, chapters cover: audio plugin architecture and the host/plugin API models (RackAFX, VST3, AU); oscillator design (including bandlimited waveform generation to avoid aliasing); envelope generators (ADSR and variants); LFOs and modulation routing; filter design (multiple topologies including the Moog ladder, state-variable, and biquad filters); voice architecture and polyphony/voice-stealing; and effects processing. It is written for programmers with working C++ knowledge who want to build real, shippable synth plugins — it assumes programming competence (classes, inheritance, real-time constraints) that most other books in this library do not, and is unambiguously a professional/serious-hobbyist DSP engineering text rather than a musician's conceptual guide. For SYNTHBUILDER, this is the single most directly relevant technical resource in the entire library: it is a from-scratch, code-level guide to building exactly the kind of synthesizer plugin SYNTHBUILDER's VST3/JUCE phase aims at (per SYNTHBUILDER's own CLAUDE.md, JSFX now, 'eventually VST3/JUCE'), including working, named implementations of core DSP building blocks (oscillators, envelopes, filters including the Moog ladder) that could be ported to JSFX's simpler scripting language or directly adapted for a future VST3/JUCE build.

West, one of the twentieth century's most eminent classicists (renowned for work on Greek epic, lyric poetry, and Near Eastern influences on Greek literature), the book tackles a genuinely difficult evidentiary problem: almost no continuous notated Greek music survives, so reconstruction depends on piecing together scattered literary references (Plato and Aristotle's philosophical discussions of musical modes and their ethical/psychological effects, technical treatises like those of Aristoxenus), a small number of inscriptions and papyrus fragments preserving actual musical notation, depictions of instruments in vase painting and sculpture, and surviving instrument fragments themselves (auloi, lyres, kitharas). West systematically works through the surviving notational system (a letter-based notation distinct from and much older than modern staff notation), the Greek theoretical understanding of scales, modes (harmoniai), and tuning systems (the tetrachord as the basic building block, various genera — diatonic, chromatic, enharmonic), rhythm and meter's relationship to poetic meter, instruments and their construction/tuning, and the few substantial surviving musical fragments (such as the Delphic Hymns and the Seikilos epitaph), offering his own transcriptions into modern notation where the evidence allows. It is written for classicists, musicologists, and advanced students with some background in Greek (quotations are often given in the original) and music theory; it is not an accessible introduction but a rigorous scholarly reconstruction. For SYNTHBUILDER this book has no direct technical relevance — no synthesis, DSP, or modern sound technology content — but its deep engagement with alternative tuning systems, modal theory, and the tetrachord-based Greek scalar system is a genuinely interesting resource if SYNTHBUILDER or a sibling project ever wanted to implement historically informed microtonal or non-equal-tempered tuning tables in a JSFX synth, a technically feasible and musically distinctive direction the project's docs do not currently pursue.
relevance_to_synthbuilder: Low — a classical-philology reconstruction of ancient Greek music theory and notation; no technical content, only a distant potential source for historically informed microtonal tuning experiments.

The book is organized in two parts. Part I, 'Sound and Hearing,' moves chronologically and thematically through the philosophy and physiology of auditory perception: Alan Towey on Aristotle and Alexander of Aphrodisias's account of hearing and instantaneous change; Elizabeth Sears on the iconography of auditory perception in early medieval psalm illustration and exegesis; Charles Burnett himself on 'Sound and its Perception in the Middle Ages'; Thomas Frangenberg on Charles de Bovelles's Renaissance comparison of hearing and vision (Auditus visu prestantior — 'hearing more excellent than sight'); Penelope Gouk on English theories of hearing in the seventeenth century before and after Descartes; and Paolo Gozza on a mechanical account of hearing from the 'Galilean school,' focused on Pietro Mengoli's 1670 Speculationi di Musica. Part II, 'Musical Judgement,' covers Andrew Barker on Plato and Aristoxenus on the nature of melos (melody/pitch-motion); John Caldwell on the concept of musical judgment in Late Antiquity; Klaus-Jürgen Sachs on Boethius and 'the judgement of the ears' as a hidden challenge running through medieval and Renaissance music theory; and Michael Fend on the changing functions of senso and ragione (sense and reason) in late-sixteenth-century Italian music theory. A select bibliography and two indices (nominum, rerum) close the volume. This is rigorous history-of-science/history-of-ideas scholarship, written for historians of philosophy, science, and music theory — it assumes graduate-level familiarity with the relevant primary sources (often quoted in Latin/Greek/Italian) and offers no accessible summary for general readers.
